title: What Will the Night Sky Look Like When Gliese 710 Arrives?
description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

At closest approach in about 1.3 million years, the orange dwarf Gliese 710 will become the brightest star in the night sky — about three times brighter than Sirius, as bright as Jupiter at its best — and creep across the sky by the width of the full Moon every 35 years.

Sources: Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — peak brightness at magnitude −2.7 (about 3× brighter than Sirius) and perihelion proper motion of 52.28″/yr (~1 full-Moon width every 35.6 years) (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a).

Pictures: ESO La Silla night-sky and star-trails time-lapses by S. Brunier and R. Wesson (CC BY 4.0), NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA WISE infrared sky photograph, NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS Juno colour-enhanced photograph of Jupiter (PIA21974), and NASA/GSFC/ASU Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter full-Moon photograph, alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: ESO/S. Brunier; R. Wesson/ESO; NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA; NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS; NASA/GSFC/ASU.
